**Chinese Communist Party (CCP) General Secretary Xi Jinping has expanded his military purges, expelling nine of the seniormost generals from the CCP and referring them to military procuratorates for criminal prosecution.

The purge is part of a major restructuring of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) leadership and reflects Xi’s continued doubt about the political loyalty of the military elite.**The PRC Ministry of National Defense announced the expulsion of the generals from the party and military on October 17.[1] The generals are listed here with their most recent titles before removal.
Some or all were removed from their posts before the announcement on October 17.

PRC officials and state media claimed that these nine individuals “seriously violated party discipline and were suspected of serious duty-related crimes involving an extremely large amount of money, of extremely serious nature, and with extremely detrimental consequences.”[2] The Ministry of National Defense spokesperson called the expulsion a “significant achievement in the party and military’s anti-corruption campaign” and claimed that it would lead to a more cohesive and combat-ready PLA.

Eight of the nine generals were members of the CCP Central Committee and were replaced during the Central Committee’s Fourth Plenum from October 20 to 23, though the PRC has not announced replacements for most of them in their military roles.[3] The Fourth Plenum elevated General Zhang Shengmin to replace He Weidong as CMC second-ranked vice chairman, however.
Zhang is already on the CMC as its Commission for Discipline Inspection (CDI) secretary.

The Fourth Plenum did not announce that Zhang would be leaving his role as CMC CDI secretary and did not add any new members to the CMC, suggesting that he may hold both positions at least temporarily.

The Fourth Plenum also announced the expulsion of alternate Central Committee member Lieutenant General Zhang Fengzhong—the PLA Rocket Force’s Political Office director—who was not previously confirmed to be under investigation.
The expulsion of the nine generals marks one of the largest purges of senior military officials in Xi Jinping’s longstanding “anti-corruption” campaign.

He Weidong is the first sitting CMC vice chairman to be purged since Zhao Ziyang in 1989 and the first uniformed vice chairman to be purged since He Long in 1967.[4] The removal of He Weidong and Miao Hua, together with former Defense Minister Li Shangfu in 2023, has reduced the CMC from seven members to four in just two years, possibly narrowing the inner circle on which Xi relies for military decision making.
The generals expelled on October 17 are part of a larger group of senior officers across all parts of the military whom the CCP has investigated or punished since late 2024.

Taiwanese National Security Bureau (NSB) Director Tsai Ming-yen reported on October 15 that over half of the 35 PLA generals (including three lieutenant generals acting as full generals) have been absent from public view for the past six months and 16 of them since December 2024.[5] The generals purged on October 17 included top leaders in all PLA services except the Air Force, but leaders in every service and theater command have been targeted by anti-corruption authorities since late 2024.

This wave of purges appears to be separate from anti-corruption investigations that targeted the PLA Rocket Force and equipment procurement in 2023, removing the PLA Rocket Force commander and two defense ministers.

**The near-total purge of the Fujian Clique from the PLA has removed many of the seniormost officers with experience focused on Taiwan.**It is unclear what effect that will have on PLA planning and readiness, however, as the CCP may yet replace the generals with others with experience focused on Taiwan.
It is possible that disagreement over Taiwan policy was a factor in the recent purges, though CDOT-ISW has not observed direct evidence of that.

**The purge of the generals is likely connected to Xi Jinping’s continued push to centralize control of the military under his personal leadership and enforce ideological orthodoxy.**A frontpage editorial in the official PLA newspaper _PLA Daily_ on October 18 accused the purged generals of undermining CCP leadership of the PLA, the CMC Chairman Responsibility System, and the “political and ideological foundation for unity and progress” within the PLA.[13] It specifically named He Weidong, Miao Hua, and He Hongjun and stated that their corruption is a “mutated form of the pernicious influence of Guo Boxiong and Xu Caihou.”[14] The Chairman Responsibility system is a concept the CCP introduced in 2014—in contrast to a previous “Vice Chairman Responsibility System”—referring to the ultimate authority of CMC Chairman Xi Jinping over the military.[15] Guo Boxiong and Xu Caihou were CMC vice chairmen under Xi’s predecessor Hu Jintao.

They were arrested and expelled from the party in 2014 for bribery and corruption, having already retired from the CMC.[16] Retired PLA officers noted at the time that Xi likely introduced the Chairman Responsibility System based on his impression that Xu and Guo had usurped Hu Jintao’s power.

The officers said that Xu and Guo had served as proxies for Jiang Zemin—the CCP general secretary before Hu—thus undermining Hu while he was in office.[17] _PLA Daily’s_ comparison of He Weidong, Miao Hua, and He Hongjun to Xu and Guo suggests that Xi was concerned that the recently purged generals could similarly undermine his authority.

Recent PRC directives and publications have shown that Xi and CCP leaders are trying to defend the Chairman Responsibility System against not only corruption and self-interest, but possibly also ideological challengers.

The PRC issued directives in February 2025 that strengthened oversight of military-related publications after multiple PLA-affiliated organizations published articles that emphasized tenets of collective leadership and intra-party democracy—principles that challenge the Chairman Responsibility System.[18] _PLA Daily_ published a series of commentary articles in July 2025 stressing the military’s subservience to the party with Xi Jinping at the core.[19] The newspaper also announced new regulations, which were not published in full, that likewise emphasized strengthening party control over the military and promoting personnel based on merit rather than personal relationships.[20] Four of the generals purged on October 17—Miao Hua, He Hongjun, Qin Shutong, and Yuan Huazhi—were top political commissars, responsible for enforcing political discipline and loyalty to the CCP within the military.
Their removal could be due to ideological disagreements with Xi’s directives or failure to enforce them to Xi’s satisfaction.

Several of the purged generals were promoted as replacements for other purged top officials, indicating that Xi’s earlier rounds of purges did not successfully remove disloyalty or corruption in the military.
Miao Hua replaced Zhang Yang as the CMC top political commissar in 2017 after Zhang committed suicide while facing an anti-corruption investigation.

Wang Houbin replaced Li Yuchao as PLA Rocket Force commander in 2023, after Li was removed as part of a wave of anti-corruption investigations targeting the PLA Rocket Force and equipment procurement departments.

**Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo expressed doubt on October 21 that Taiwan would receive the 66 F-16V fighter jets that it purchased from Lockheed Martin by 2026, as originally agreed.

Delayed acquisition of US systems will likely contribute to greater “America skepticism” within Taiwan and contribute to existing narratives surrounding US “exploitation” of Taiwan.**Koo said that the jet delivery program had encountered delays, which may prevent the purchased jets from arriving on time.[45] Taiwan purchased the jets for approximately 245.38 billion NTD (8 billion US dollars) in August 2020, with final delivery expected by 2026.[46] Taiwan has received none of the jets at the time of this reporting.[47] This incident is part of a series of delays in US weapons deliveries to Taiwan.

The Taiwan Security Monitor estimated that the backlog of US weapons sold but not delivered to Taiwan as of September 2025 is approximately 21.5 billion US dollars.[48] Delays have impacted Taiwan’s acquisitions of munitions, traditional platforms, and asymmetric capabilities from the United States, which harms Taiwan’s ability to enhance its military capabilities and defend against PRC aggression.
The PRC and some Taiwanese politicians can use delayed deliveries of US equipment to bolster narratives that weaken US-Taiwanese relations.

Taiwanese politicians frequently issue complaints when US weapons delays are announced, criticizing the United States for pushing Taiwan to purchase expensive weapons systems that take a long time to receive.
This discourse contributes to broader trends of “America skepticism” within Taiwan, which questions the likelihood of US assistance in a Taiwan contingency.

KMT legislator Ma Wen-chun questioned the decision to purchase the F-16s on October 21 and called the delay “unacceptable.” [49] The spread of such narratives within the KMT, which has effective control over the LY, could lead to Taiwan becoming less likely to purchase new weapons systems from the United States and harm US-Taiwanese relations overall.
National Security Bureau (NSB) Director General Tsai Ming-yen said on October 15 during an LY interpellation that the PRC is increasing espionage efforts in Taiwan.

The PRC is known to have tried to influence political parties across Taiwan’s political spectrum, including but not limited to funding the fringe China Unification Promotion Party, recruiting former DPP aides for espionage, funding a hometown association trip targeting KMT wardens, and more.
The NSB statements reflect Taiwan’s growing awareness and expanding efforts to counter such PRC efforts.

**The CCP held the fourth plenary session of its 20 th Central Committee from October 20 to 23 and released its 15 th Five Year Plan (FYP) that will guide PRC economic, technological, and military development through 2030.

The 15 th FYP signals a continuation of PRC modernization efforts.**The CCP Constitution requires an annual plenum to convene the CCP Central Committee—the highest CCP authority—to discuss policy issues.

In a communiqué, this plenary session outlined the 15 th FYP, which seeks to improve PRC economic strength, scientific and technological advancement, national defense capabilities, comprehensive national power, quality of life for the Chinese people, and international influence.
A more detailed proposal for achieving the 15 th FYP’s goals is expected to be released in a week and will be passed during the two 2026 sessions.
